passages.original: Istis autem mechanica gaudet maritari, mediocribus politica.Excellenter vero auctorum tres invenimus partitiones, quorum quidam sunt excel- lenter acuti, alii mediocres, tertii excellentissime acuti. Excellenter acutis gaudet œconomica, me- diocribus vero sub lunari globo physica, apotheca- riorumque practica. Excellentissime acutis, quos maxime Aristoteles notos secundum philosophiam vocat, universalium per experimenta singularium arridet cognitio ;.hæc trivialium domina est, qua- drivialium potentia. o quam est felix exhibitio ! Mediocritatis tamen extrema partitio, bonos perfe- ctosque licet sibi quandoque comparavit cum su- dore.magistratus tamen dotati sunt honore consum- pto flore juventæ.
passages.english: With these [the slow], mechanics is glad to be wedded; with the middling, politics. Among the excellent, however, we find three divisions of authors: some are excellently sharp, others middling, and a third group most excellently sharp. Economics delights in the excellently sharp; in the middling, physics of the region beneath the lunar sphere, and the practice of apothecaries. To the most excellently sharp, whom Aristotle calls those most known according to philosophy, the knowledge of universals through experience of particulars is pleasing; this is the mistress of the trivium subjects and the power of the quadrivium subjects. O how happy a display it is! Yet the lowest division, that of middling ability, although it has at times acquired good and accomplished men for itself, [does so] with sweat; they are endowed with the honour of the mastership only when the flower of youth has been spent.
passages.notes: The opening 'Istis' presumably refers to the mediocre or obtuse mentioned in the preceding context; the referent is unclear. The passage is awkward and possibly corrupt: 'auctorum' may stand for 'acutorum' ("of the sharp"). 'Magistratus' here seems to mean the academic mastership rather than civic office. The last sentence's construction is uncertain.

passages.original: Istis tamen siquidem prædictis hoc modo est ordinandum : primo ut sciat quisque ad tanti nominis pertineant reverentiam, ut quæ scita sunt exprimere noscat,et ne scriptorum commissiuni se totaliter committat, ut Lucretius, qui cujuslibet quæstionis modum propositæ inquirendo, dimisso comitatu schedulis confluebat. Secundo ut librorum copiam suæ acquirat exercitatiuni, ut cum opus fuerit eos consulat. Nec omnino eis in credat, ut Jugo qui Montani sui magistri monitis tantum confisus est, quod omne verbum ab ipsius ore progressum quaternullis exarabat et tanquam sacrum existima- bat, nil aliud quam magistri vicem in scholis obtinens prædicabat, unde multoties pudore confusus inclu- sus abibat.
passages.english: With these things said beforehand, matters must be arranged in this way. First, that each person should know what pertains to the reverence owed to so great a name, so that he may know how to express what he has learned, and that he should not entrust himself wholly to the keeping of writings, like Lucretius, who, in investigating the manner of any question set before him, abandoned company and flocked to his notes. Second, that he should acquire a supply of books for his own exercise, so that he may consult them when there is need. Nor should he believe them entirely, like Jugo, who trusted so much in the advice of his master Montanus that he wrote down in little quires every word that came from his mouth and regarded it as sacred; when holding his master's place in the schools he preached nothing else, and so many times he went off shut away, confounded with shame.
passages.notes: 'commissiuni' and 'exercitatiuni' read as 'commissioni' and 'exercitationi'; 'in credat' as 'credat' (or 'increduat'); 'quaternullis' as 'quaternulis' (little quires). 'Lucretius' here is evidently not the poet, and 'Jugo' and 'Montanus' are unidentified. 'confluebat' ("flocked") is odd for a single person and may be corrupt. 'inclusus abibat' is obscure.
